frictionVectors.title: European gas leverage
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian gas while seeking alternative suppliers, creating bargaining opportunities but also pressure over pricing, migration, and long-term contracts.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign energy competition
frictionVectors.details: International firms remain important in upstream investment and technology, but Sonatrach retains dominant control over strategic energy assets.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector external dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining production, foreign operators, and reliance on external capital constrain Luanda's ability to convert hydrocarbons into broader sovereign industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-for-infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction relationships support transport infrastructure but can narrow fiscal flexibility and reinforce commodity-linked repayment risks.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou's role as a regional gateway is strategically valuable, but dependence on external logistics, financing, and neighboring market access limits full national control.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity near the northern borders threatens transport corridors, agricultural production, and state access to frontier resources.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains substantial influence over diamond governance, but dependence on global demand and major trading partners leaves revenues exposed to market shifts.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in copper, nickel, and other minerals is increasing, creating opportunities for diversification while testing the country's regulatory and negotiating capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The authorities are seeking greater state participation, local processing, and revenue capture from gold, increasing friction with foreign operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security alignment
frictionVectors.details: Closer security cooperation with Russia may reduce reliance on Western partners, but opaque arrangements and continued insurgency complicate control over mining zones and transport routes.

frictionVectors.title: Opaque Mineral Licensing
frictionVectors.details: Gold and rare-earth projects remain vulnerable to opaque licensing, informal exports, and foreign intermediaries. Limited state capacity weakens Burundi's ability to capture revenue and enforce local processing.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Strained relations with Rwanda and reliance on regional security arrangements constrain sovereign decision-making. Cross-border militia activity also threatens transport and trade corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Mindelo and Praia remain attractive to external investors and security partners seeking Atlantic logistics access. Concession terms and strategic port use require careful balancing among European, Chinese, and wider international interests.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, connectivity, and renewable-energy projects depend heavily on external finance. Debt sustainability and foreign ownership can limit domestic control over critical infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Resource Chains
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber, and emerging mining projects are shaped by foreign firms and opaque subcontracting networks. Weak transparency and limited processing capacity reduce Cameroon's sovereign capture of resource value.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Northern Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside extremist violence in the Far North, disrupts roads, plantations, and border trade. Insecurity increases dependence on external security, finance, and infrastructure partners.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and Diamond Capture
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups, foreign security contractors, and informal networks compete for control of gold and diamonds. The state's limited territorial reach makes transparent licensing and revenue collection extremely difficult.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bangui relies heavily on Russian security support while maintaining ties with regional and international partners. Security-linked commercial arrangements risk exchanging short-term regime protection for long-term resource and infrastructure concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Oil Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Oil exports through the Cameroon pipeline remain central to state revenue and vulnerable to foreign operators, transit arrangements, and price volatility. Limited diversification weakens Chad's bargaining power over infrastructure and fiscal terms.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan and Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan war and instability across the Sahel pressure border security, refugee systems, and trade routes. Chad's strategic value to external military and security partners can bring support while narrowing policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Mayotte sovereignty dispute
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, while Moroni continues to reject its separation and faces domestic pressure over migration and consular restrictions.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and remittance dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited domestic revenues leave infrastructure and energy projects dependent on external donors, Gulf partners, and diaspora remittances.

highlights: Eastern sovereignty is under military pressure

frictionVectors.title: Mining-contract asymmetry
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt output is strategically important, but foreign operators and opaque contract structures continue to limit Kinshasa's effective control over value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern security and mineral corridors
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and other armed groups disrupts state authority and trade routes, with regional and external actors accused of shaping access to mineral zones.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains heavily dependent on oil production and foreign technical and commercial partners, exposing fiscal sovereignty to price cycles and contract terms.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, rail, and other projects improve connectivity but increase exposure to repayment pressures and externally controlled procurement and construction chains.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa-sector external dependence
frictionVectors.details: Processing capacity and regulatory reforms are improving domestic value capture, but farmers and exporters remain exposed to global firms, volatile prices, and sustainability rules set abroad.

frictionVectors.title: Port and strategic investment competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port and logistics expansion attracts French, Chinese, Gulf, and other investors, creating leverage benefits while raising concerns over long-term control of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military footprint
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities generate revenue and security guarantees but limit Djibouti's room for independent strategic maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked port and logistics infrastructure is central to the economy, while debt exposure and regional competition complicate national control over critical trade assets.

highlights: Suez and LNG remain strategic lifelines
GERD diplomacy stays locked with Ethiopia

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Gulf Capital Dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-backed reforms and major Gulf investments are stabilizing Egypt’s finances while increasing external leverage over strategic assets and land. Cairo retains formal control but faces pressure to monetize state holdings.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Water Security
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved dispute over Ethiopia’s GERD continues to threaten Egypt’s core water security. Negotiations remain constrained by limited enforcement mechanisms and wider regional rivalries.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Decline
frictionVectors.details: Maturing oil and gas fields are reducing export revenues and narrowing the government’s fiscal room. Foreign operators remain important for technical capacity, leaving the state exposed to production and investment decisions beyond its control.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-Linked Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large externally financed construction projects have expanded state infrastructure but created long-term repayment and contractor dependence. Economic diversification remains limited despite official industrialization plans.

highlights: Mining remains the principal hard-currency source
Red Sea access raises strategic value

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Copper, zinc and gold projects provide vital revenues but depend on foreign capital, equipment and marketing networks. Limited transparency around concessions and state participation complicates assessment of how much value remains domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea’s coastline is increasingly affected by competition involving Gulf states, Yemen-related insecurity and broader maritime rivalries. External security interest creates bargaining leverage but also risks turning access arrangements into strategic dependency.

highlights: South African trade routes remain indispensable
Sugar and forestry face market pressure

frictionVectors.title: South African Economic Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African transport corridors, electricity links, customs arrangements and investment. This provides resilience but limits independent control over critical supply chains and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Industrial and Fiscal Fragility
frictionVectors.details: The country’s manufacturing base and public finances remain vulnerable to regional trade volatility and dependence on shared-revenue mechanisms. External investors retain significant influence over export-oriented agriculture and processing.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Standoff
frictionVectors.details: The GERD has increased Ethiopia’s leverage over regional power and water politics, but tensions with Egypt and Sudan remain unresolved. Dam operations and future electricity exports are vulnerable to diplomatic escalation.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance and Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, IMF engagement and reliance on foreign contractors create pressure to liberalize strategic sectors and prioritize creditor confidence. China, Gulf investors and Western institutions all compete for influence over infrastructure and logistics.

highlights: Post-coup transition seeks tighter control over oil and mining
French influence recalibrates as Chinese capital expands

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are pressing for greater state participation and domestic value addition in oil, manganese, and timber. Investors remain attentive to contract stability and the pace of political normalization.

frictionVectors.title: External influence competition
frictionVectors.details: France is losing some privileged access while Chinese and other non-Western partners pursue infrastructure and extractive opportunities. Libreville is balancing diversification against dependence on foreign capital and expertise.

highlights: Senegal remains the essential security and trade partner
Cashew, fisheries, and tourism expose weak bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for transport corridors, food supply, energy links, and security cooperation. This improves stability but limits Banjul's room to negotiate independently on infrastructure and trade.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and maritime enforcement
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing pressure and limited monitoring capacity continue to threaten coastal resources and local livelihoods. Partnerships with European and regional actors provide support but do not fully restore sovereign control.

highlights: Debt stabilization is tied to IMF-backed reforms
Gold remains powerful, while illegal mining damages state capacity

frictionVectors.title: Gold and illegal mining
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale and informal mining generate revenue but also drive environmental damage, corruption, and local conflict. The state is seeking tighter oversight while remaining dependent on the sector for foreign exchange.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is courting outside capital for lithium and other minerals while trying to secure local processing and better fiscal terms. Debt pressures and infrastructure needs weaken its negotiating leverage with multinational investors.

highlights: Bauxite exports underpin junta-era infrastructure ambitions
Simandou could transform the country's resource geography

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor control
frictionVectors.details: The rail, port, and iron-ore project is drawing major Chinese and international investment, creating jobs and infrastructure but also long-term dependency risks. Guinea's leverage depends on enforcing local-content, revenue, and environmental commitments.

frictionVectors.title: Junta legitimacy and contract risk
frictionVectors.details: The military government uses mining revenues to support its political project while delaying a full return to civilian rule. Sanctions risk, opaque contracting, and social tensions could complicate future resource governance.

highlights: Cashew exports remain the core economic lifeline
Political instability constrains independent resource policy

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country exports most cashews with limited processing, leaving farmers and state finances exposed to foreign buyers and price swings. Efforts to build domestic processing face weak electricity, finance, and transport infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and political vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's port and transport networks are vulnerable to external commercial influence and domestic power struggles. Persistent institutional fragility limits the government's ability to negotiate durable, sovereign infrastructure and fisheries agreements.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Heavy debt-service obligations and reliance on Chinese, Gulf, and Western financing limit Nairobi's policy room. Major transport and energy projects remain vulnerable to refinancing conditions and foreign contractor interests.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Security
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and LAPSSET corridor remain strategically important but face insecurity, local land disputes, and uneven commercial demand. These constraints complicate Kenya's effort to consolidate control over its Indian Ocean gateway.

frictionVectors.title: South African Water Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's fiscal position and infrastructure planning remain closely tied to water exports under the Lesotho Highlands Water Project. South Africa's dominant market and financing role limits Maseru's bargaining power over this strategic resource.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Owned Textile Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The garment sector provides vital employment but is heavily exposed to foreign investors, imported inputs, and shifting trade preferences. Weak domestic value addition leaves Lesotho vulnerable to external commercial decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concession Control
frictionVectors.details: Large iron ore operations and associated rail and port infrastructure are dominated by multinational concession holders. The government faces pressure to increase royalties, local processing, and transparency without deterring investment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Liberia relies on external financing and operators for roads, energy, and port modernization. This accelerates development but can transfer long-term control of strategic infrastructure away from domestic institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and armed networks continue to contest control over production, export terminals, and public spending. The National Oil Corporation remains a key national institution but operates under persistent political and regional pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Entrenchment
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked forces, and other external actors retain influence through security partnerships, equipment, and local alliances. Their presence constrains Libya's sovereign control over bases, borders, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and export-oriented infrastructure. Madagascar is seeking greater fiscal and local-development returns while managing environmental and community opposition.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel and Power Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and reliance on imported fuel expose the country to external price and financing shocks. Weak domestic infrastructure reduces the government's leverage over large mining and logistics investors.

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and value capture
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking foreign capital for uranium, rare earths and other mineral projects, but limited processing capacity risks leaving value and strategic control offshore.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel and power vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported fuel, constrained foreign exchange and unreliable electricity expose national infrastructure and food systems to external supply shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: The breakdown with France and Western partners has increased reliance on Russian-linked security support, creating new leverage over military and strategic decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining disputes and fiscal pressure
frictionVectors.details: The state is pressing foreign gold operators for a larger share of revenues, but regulatory disputes and insecurity threaten production, investment and sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore gas partnership tensions
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal offers major fiscal upside, but cross-border governance, revenue allocation and security coordination remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of extractive logistics
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and emerging gas infrastructure rely heavily on international operators, finance and export corridors, limiting immediate domestic value capture.

highlights: Port strategy balances India and China

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty transition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues to seek effective control and economic benefit from the Chagos Archipelago, while the Diego Garcia security facility preserves powerful external strategic interests.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Port, digital and maritime-security partnerships with India, China and Western states create investment opportunities but require careful protection of strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is expanding infrastructure and resource development in Western Sahara, but sovereignty claims remain contested and expose projects to legal, diplomatic and reputational pressure.

frictionVectors.title: EU market and investment dependence
frictionVectors.details: European trade, finance and industrial partnerships are vital to Morocco's green-energy and manufacturing ambitions, giving outside actors influence over strategic sectors.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado LNG security
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency remains the principal obstacle to restoring major gas exports. Mozambique relies heavily on foreign operators and external security assistance, limiting direct sovereign control over project timelines and revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Megaproject dependence
frictionVectors.details: LNG, mining, and transport infrastructure are dominated by foreign capital and contractors. Debt exposure and revenue-sharing arrangements constrain Maputo's fiscal leverage.

highlights: Oil and green hydrogen reshape strategy

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of new energy assets
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil discoveries and green-hydrogen projects could transform Namibia, but development depends on international majors, technology, and financing. Local-content rules will determine whether resource sovereignty improves materially.

frictionVectors.title: Export-corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Namibia is positioning Walvis Bay as a gateway for landlocked neighbors while competing with South African and regional corridors. Port expansion and logistics partnerships may create strategic dependence on external operators.

highlights: Sahel alliance redirects trade and defense

frictionVectors.title: Russian security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Niger's break with France and reduced Western military presence has increased reliance on Russian-linked security support. This may expand regime autonomy while introducing new dependency and accountability risks.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and export-route pressure
frictionVectors.details: Resource nationalism over uranium and hydrocarbons is constrained by weak security, limited processing capacity, and reliance on neighboring transit states. Relations with Benin and other coastal corridors remain strategically important.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Delta production insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, pipeline vandalism, and local grievances continue to reduce output and public revenue. Foreign operators remain central to upstream production while the state struggles to enforce infrastructure control.

frictionVectors.title: Power and infrastructure financing
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and transport bottlenecks constrain industrial sovereignty. Chinese, Gulf, and Western financing can accelerate projects but may deepen long-term exposure to external capital and contractual obligations.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC conflict
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's alleged support for M23 has generated severe diplomatic pressure and threatens relations with the DRC and international partners. Regional security influence provides leverage but carries sanctions and reputational risks.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-mineral scrutiny
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role as a mineral trading and transit hub is facing intensified demands for traceability. Dependence on external markets and aid partners limits Kigali's room to dismiss international compliance pressure.

frictionVectors.title: UNCERTAIN OFFSHORE LICENSING
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe retains formal control over prospective offshore blocks, but limited technical and financial capacity leaves licensing terms vulnerable to external partners and neighboring maritime claims.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL INFRASTRUCTURE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Port, energy, and connectivity projects depend heavily on foreign financing and contractors, constraining the state's bargaining space without yet producing a dominant external sphere of control.

frictionVectors.title: CONTRACT RENEGOTIATION PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater domestic value capture from oil, gas, and mining projects, creating friction with international operators and investors over contract stability, local content, and revenue sharing.

frictionVectors.title: GTA CROSS-BORDER GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: The shared Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas project with Mauritania requires sustained bilateral coordination on maritime security, revenue allocation, and domestic processing expectations.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN TUNA FLEETS
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from fisheries licensing and processing but remains exposed to unequal bargaining power with distant-water fleets, raising concerns over stock sustainability and retained value.

frictionVectors.title: STRATEGIC INFRASTRUCTURE COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Indian, Chinese, European, and Gulf partners compete for maritime, port, and security access, requiring careful balancing to preserve Seychelles' policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, bauxite, and emerging critical-mineral projects provide essential revenue but leave the state exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and disputes over fiscal terms and land access.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND INFRASTRUCTURE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed transport and mining infrastructure can improve export capacity while reinforcing an enclave model unless local processing, procurement, and environmental safeguards are strengthened.

frictionVectors.title: FEDERAL RESOURCE JURISDICTION
frictionVectors.details: Disputes between the federal government and member states over offshore hydrocarbons, licensing authority, and revenue sharing weaken Somalia's ability to negotiate unified and transparent resource agreements.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL SECURITY AND PORT INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other external actors provide security, port, and infrastructure support, but competing access arrangements risk entrenching fragmented sovereignty and tying strategic assets to outside patrons.

frictionVectors.title: Mining ownership and beneficiation
frictionVectors.details: Pretoria is seeking greater domestic processing and leverage over platinum, manganese and rare-earth supply chains, while foreign investors resist regulatory uncertainty and local-content demands.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and freight infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability has improved unevenly, but port and rail constraints continue to limit sovereign control over exports and raise dependence on private and external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Oil transit dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on Sudanese pipelines and export terminals, leaving its revenue and production vulnerable to conflict, transit disputes and outside political leverage.

frictionVectors.title: External security and aid dependence
frictionVectors.details: International peacekeeping, humanitarian financing and neighboring-state mediation remain essential, limiting Juba's autonomy while political competition threatens infrastructure security.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and wartime supply chains
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling provide revenue to armed actors and attract regional and external intermediaries, weakening civilian control over strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Port and pipeline vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Fighting and political fragmentation threaten Port Sudan, oil infrastructure and humanitarian corridors, increasing dependence on foreign mediation and security guarantees.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and gas contract leverage
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is pressing for local participation, revenue transparency and domestic processing in mining and gas, creating periodic tension with multinational operators.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic transport corridors
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port and energy projects are drawing competing Chinese, Gulf and Western interest, giving Dodoma leverage but increasing exposure to external financing and geopolitical rivalry.

highlights: Lomé consolidates as a regional hub

frictionVectors.title: Port-centered external influence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé's deep-water port and logistics networks attract foreign capital and regional trade, but dependence on external operators and financing limits full sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security corridor
frictionVectors.details: Militant spillover from the Sahel is pressuring border security and transport routes, increasing reliance on foreign security cooperation and diverting resources from development.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration-security dependency
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give Brussels significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Domestic opposition to external conditionality remains politically potent.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import exposure
frictionVectors.details: Tunisia remains vulnerable to imported gas and electricity, particularly through links with Algeria and Europe. Declining phosphate performance further limits autonomous foreign-exchange capacity.

highlights: Oil wealth tied to external capital

frictionVectors.title: EACOP geopolitical contest
frictionVectors.details: The China-backed East African Crude Oil Pipeline remains central to Uganda's resource strategy but faces sustained environmental and human-rights criticism from Western governments and civil society.

frictionVectors.title: Critical infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's oil, transport, and power expansion relies heavily on foreign financing and contractors. This increases state capacity while limiting independent control over project terms and revenue timing.

frictionVectors.title: Copper ownership competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf-linked investors to seek better terms in copper and cobalt. Processing capacity and revenue transparency remain weaker than the country's bargaining ambitions.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has reduced immediate pressure but leaves fiscal policy influenced by creditors and multilateral institutions. Rail, power, and logistics bottlenecks continue to constrain sovereign mineral control.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral value-chain contest
frictionVectors.details: Harare is restricting exports of unprocessed lithium and seeking domestic beneficiation, but Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in mining and processing. Limited finance and technology weaken the state's ability to capture higher-value rents.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and payment isolation
frictionVectors.details: U.S. and other Western sanctions, alongside restricted access to conventional finance, push Zimbabwe toward opaque bilateral deals and alternative payment channels. This reduces transparency and increases dependence on a narrower group of external partners.
